​Introduction​
​For the ASNE PEP 2026 Unmanned-autonomy competition, our team of 11 senior​
​Mechanical Engineering undergraduate students is participating on behalf of the University of​
​Illinois at Urbana-Champaign as a part of our senior design project. This report highlights our​
​background research into the underlying Engineering, Physics, and Control algorithms required​
​to build an unmanned-autonomous boat capable of participating in the competition.​
​Our team consists of 5 members who worked on the boat in Fall 2025, and 6 members​
​who are currently working on the boat this semester. This project provides benefits beyond​
​competition performance by establishing a reusable technical foundation for future teams and​
​strengthening interdisciplinary experience in marine systems design, autonomous control, and​
​electric propulsion engineering.​

​Background Research​
​Our background research for this project evaluates current trends in autonomous control​
​systems, hull designs, and electric propulsion, to establish a technical baseline for marine​
​autonomous surface vehicle (ASV) development. Through analysis of these key technologies, we​
​were able to address fundamental engineering questions on the necessary navigation and control​
​strategies to adapt and implement for marine operating environments, sensing architectures to​
​enable reliable localization during high-speed operation, and sensor fusion robustness under​
​environmental disturbances. It further examines performance in the planing regime—a​
​high-speed operating condition in which hydrodynamic lift raises the hull and reduces drag—and​
​evaluates which hull geometries provide efficient and stable behavior, how hydrodynamic​
​response affects structural loading requirements, and where reinforcement is most critical to​
​withstand slamming and sustained planing loads without unnecessary weight. Finally, propulsion​
​system considerations are evaluated by investigating how propeller sizing, drivetrain​
​configuration, and rudder selection influence thrust generation, maneuverability, and overall​
​operational reliability, providing insight to guide the design decisions presented in this work.​

​craft, with emphasis on achieving efficient operation under payload and stability constraints.​

​Background Research​
       ​Our background research for this project evaluates current trends in autonomous control​
​systems, hull designs, and electric propulsion, to establish a technical baseline for marine​
​autonomous surface vehicle (ASV) development. Through analysis of these key technologies, we​
​were able to address fundamental engineering questions on the necessary navigation and control​
​strategies to adapt and implement for marine operating environments, sensing architectures to​
​enable reliable localization during high-speed operation, and sensor fusion robustness under​
​environmental disturbances. It further examines performance in the planing regime—a​
​high-speed operating condition in which hydrodynamic lift raises the hull and reduces drag—and​
​evaluates which hull geometries provide efficient and stable behavior, how hydrodynamic​
​response affects structural loading requirements, and where reinforcement is most critical to​
​withstand slamming and sustained planing loads without unnecessary weight. Finally, propulsion​
​system considerations are evaluated by investigating how propeller sizing, drivetrain​
​configuration, and rudder selection influence thrust generation, maneuverability, and overall​
​operational reliability, providing insight to guide the design decisions presented in this work.​
​Hull Design​
       ​The hull design was determined through established principles of high-speed planing​
​craft, with emphasis on achieving efficient operation under payload and stability constraints.​
​Early concept evaluation compared displacement, catamaran, and hybrid hull configurations,​

pages.text:
​highlighting tradeoffs between manufacturability, stability, and achievable speed. Planing​
​monohulls emerged as the most effective solution for the required operating regime due to their​
​ability to generate hydrodynamic lift and reduce drag at higher speeds.​
​Literature indicates that moderately V-shaped (deep-V) hulls provide improved​
​lift-to-drag performance and directional stability compared to flatter-bottom geometries,​
​particularly in conditions where consistent tracking and controllability are required. These​
​characteristics are critical for autonomous operation, where predictable dynamic behavior​
​directly impacts navigation accuracy.​
​The hydrodynamic performance of planing hulls is commonly evaluated using the​
​Savitsky method, which provides an empirical relationship between hull geometry, operating​
​speed, and performance metrics such as trim angle, wetted surface area, lift, and resistance. This​
​framework enables rapid iteration of design parameters while maintaining physically meaningful​
​predictions, making it well suited for early-stage hull development [1].​
​Structural considerations are equally important, as planing hulls experience both​
​distributed hydrodynamic loading and localized transient effects such as slamming. Sustained​
​loads are typically concentrated along the aft wetted surface, while higher-magnitude,​
​short-duration impacts occur near the keel and forward bottom [2]. These conditions motivate​
​reinforcement strategies that prioritize load-path alignment and efficient material usage.​
​Grillage-style structures, consisting of longitudinal and transverse stiffeners, are commonly used​
​to distribute loads and increase stiffness without excessive weight [2].​
​Composite fiberglass construction is widely adopted in small marine vessels due to its​
​balance of strength, weight, and manufacturability. When combined with bonded internal​
​reinforcement, this approach provides a lightweight yet structurally capable hull suitable for​
​planing operation.​

​Electronics​
​Autonomous surface vehicles depend heavily on sensing and onboard electronics because​
​of the noisy, dynamic nature of marine environments. Unlike ground robots, boats cannot rely on​
​lane markings, stable terrain, or predictable traction. Wind, surface reflections, vibration, and​
​drift all interfere with perception and localization, so the electronics architecture of an​
​autonomous boat must be based on sensing redundancy rather than on a single sensor. Research​
​in autonomous marine navigation [4] therefore emphasizes the importance of selecting sensors​

pages.text:
​according to the operating environment and the mission objective, rather than simply​
​maximizing sensor count or complexity.​
​For a race in which the vehicle must follow a course marked by buoys over open water,​
​the most useful sensor classes are those that provide complementary information such as a global​
​reference for position, and inertial information for short-term motion estimation. That is why​
​GPS, and IMU appear repeatedly in autonomous surface vehicle research and in small-boat​
​autonomy practice. Therefore, it is common practice to use GPS and IMU sensors in autonomous​
​surface vehicles. More complex sensing systems such as LiDAR or stereo depth cameras can be​
​valuable in mapping-heavy applications, but they impose greater cost, integration burden, and​
​power demand, and their added value is limited when the task is surface navigation rather than​
​dense 3D reconstruction. For this reason, the technical baseline for a competition boat favors a​
​practical multi-sensor architecture built around robust, lightweight, and computationally​
​manageable electronics [5].​
​A second electronics consideration is that small electric boats must integrate sensing with​
​propulsion hardware under strict weight, waterproofing, and power constraints. The electronics​
​are therefore part of the broader challenge of packaging reliable autonomy into a compact marine​
​platform. Weight distribution limits the number of batteries we can have in the boat. The rating​
​of our ESCs and the connectors we used were determined by our power constraints and power​
​draw. Waterproofing helped us determine the distribution of our electronics through the boat.​

​Controls​
​The controls system was shaped by background research in maritime autonomy,​
​especially research showing that marine navigation is highly sensitive to disturbances such as​
​wind, drift, changing visual conditions, and high-speed maneuvering. Our background research​
​shows that LiDAR-only SLAM becomes less reliable in marine environments with limited​
​features and at higher speeds, while sensor fusion using GPS and IMU data through a Kalman​
​filter [7] significantly improves path-following accuracy for autonomous surface vehicles. This​
​directly supports the team’s decision to avoid a single-sensor strategy and instead use a​
​multi-sensor autonomous navigation architecture.​

       ​Thermal management is a fundamental background issue in electrically propelled marine​

pages.text:
​useful thrust; the rest appears as heat in motors, ESCs, wiring, and batteries. In small high-power​
​craft, this heat can build rapidly because the hull interior offers limited airflow and little room for​
​oversized thermal hardware. As a result, cooling is not merely a detail of implementation but a​
​central reliability concern in electric boat engineering.​
​This becomes even more important in autonomous boats, where overheated components​
​can directly result in mission failure. A crewed boat can sometimes be throttled back or corrected​
​immediately by an operator. An uncrewed boat, by contrast, must sustain safe component​
​temperatures while continuing to navigate on its own. Background work in electric propulsion​
​therefore points toward cooling strategies that use the operating environment efficiently. Because​
​the craft is already moving through water, marine vehicles can exploit that surrounding water as​
​a heat sink far more effectively than they could rely on passive air cooling alone.​
​For small racing craft, water-based cooling is attractive because it removes heat without​
​requiring large fans or bulky heat exchangers, both of which would consume space, mass, and​
​power. In order to reduce power consumption, we decided to use a rudder capable of picking up​
​water naturally, eliminating the need for a water pump.​

​Design Review​
​Hull Design​
​The hull geometry was refined from a Mosquito-class planing baseline using a​
​Savitsky-based workflow to meet propulsion and competition constraints. The final design point​
​(Figure 1) targets approximately 22 knots with a thrust requirement of ~25 lbf, corresponding to​
​a trim angle near 3.5° and a power requirement on the order of 2 hp [1]. These values define the​
​operating envelope and guide adjustments to beam, deadrise, and displacement to maintain stable​
​planing while accommodating payload and internal volume.​

pages.text:
​Figure 1.​​CAD sketch of final hull design​
​Hydrodynamic performance was evaluated using a CFD model in ANSYS​​®​ ​Fluent with a​
​three-dimensional multiphase Volume of Fluid (VOF) formulation and a RANS turbulence​
​model, a validated approach for planing-hull analysis [3]. The domain was sized to minimize​
​boundary effects, with pressure inlet and outlet conditions set to the target speed. A symmetry​
​plane reduced computational cost, and mesh refinement near the hull resolved pressure gradients​
​and boundary layer behavior. The CAD geometry was positioned at the expected steady-state​
​trim and submergence.​
​The simulation predicted a total drag of approximately 92 N (20.7 lbf), which is below​
​the analytical estimate of 25 lbf and within the range of available thrust. This suggests a larger​
​effective wetted area or displacement, indicating slower acceleration to top speed despite​
​achievable steady-state performance. The resulting pressure distribution (Figure 2) shows​
​dominant loading along the keel and aft wetted region, consistent with planing-hull loading​
​behavior [2].​

​This pressure field was used for structural evaluation in ANSYS​​®​ ​Mechanical. A​
​half-hull model was analyzed with minimal constraints, combining distributed hydrodynamic​
​pressure with an additional ~100 lb static load and gravity. The resulting stress distribution​
​(Figure 3) shows peak stresses along the keel and aft bottom surface, with values remaining​
​within allowable limits for the fiberglass structure, consistent with expected load concentration​
​regions [2].​

​These results informed the internal reinforcement strategy. As shown in Figure 4, the​
​structure consists of a grillage of longitudinal and transverse members. Longitudinal stiffeners​
​along the keel and chines align with primary load paths, while transverse bulkheads reduce panel​
​span and increase global stiffness, improving load distribution and limiting deformation [2].​

pages.text:
​Figure 4.​​CAD model of boat and internal structural network​
​The reinforcement network also serves as the primary structural interface for onboard​
​systems, allowing batteries, electronics, and payload to be supported through reinforced regions​
​rather than the hull skin. The spacing of stiffeners and bulkheads was influenced by packaging​
​constraints, particularly battery placement, resulting in reinforcement concentrated in the wetted​
​region where hydrodynamic loads are highest.​
​The current analysis captures steady-state hydrodynamic loading but does not include​
​transient effects such as slamming or wave impact. These dynamic loads are expected to be​
​significant, particularly in forward regions, and will be characterized through physical testing​
​prior to competition [2]. Additional reinforcement will be incorporated as needed based on​
​observed structural response, ensuring that the final hull remains robust under real operating​
​conditions while avoiding unnecessary weight.​

​Power Storage System​
​The power storage system consists of six Tattu 44.4 V 30C 12S 10000 mAh LiPo battery​
​packs divided equally between two fully isolated drive systems. Each drive system is powered by​
​three battery packs wired in parallel through a 300 A rated busbar, yielding a system capacity of​
​30 Ah at 44.4 V, or approximately 1,332 Wh per side. The parallel configuration was chosen to​
​maximize available runtime while maintaining the nominal 44.4 V required by each ESC and​
​motor pair.​

pages.text:
​Each battery pack is rated for a continuous discharge of 300 A (30 C × 10 Ah), and the​
​three-pack parallel arrangement provides a combined continuous discharge capability of 900 A​
​per side. This comfortably exceeds the 200 A continuous rating of each ESC and the 9.5 kW​
​continuous rating of each motor, which draws approximately 214 A at nominal voltage under full​
​throttle. Prior to each run, the pack state of charge is verified by checking resting cell voltage​
​before connection.​
​Each battery pack is physically restrained within an open compartment integrated into the​
​main hull structure, securing the packs against movement under wave loading and dynamic race​
​conditions. Ventilation through the open compartment arrangement allows heat generated during​
​high-rate discharge to dissipate naturally.​
​Due to the current draw by each motor under full load exceeding the rated capacity of​
​200 A, we will be cutting the maximum continuous power to be less than the available 9.5 kW​
​during racing. The 200 A circuit breaker fuse switches on each side were selected to reflect the​
​realistic peak demand of the drive system while providing overcurrent protection in the event of​
​a fault.​
​Each circuit breaker fuse switch serves a dual purpose: it acts as a manual disconnect for​
​pre-launch arming and as an automatic overcurrent cutoff during operation. A mechanical rod​
​linkage connects both killswitches, allowing a single operator action to simultaneously​
​disconnect both drive systems in an emergency.​

​Propulsion System​
​Each drive system consists of a SSS 56123 V2 brushless motor, a Hobbywing Seaking​
​200 A ESC, a flex cable drive assembly, and a 3-blade propeller. The two drive systems are​
​closely positioned along the centerline of the hull, with directional control provided primarily by​
​a single rudder rather than differential throttle.​
​The motors are 6-pole outrunner brushless motors rated for 9,500 W continuous and​
​15,800 W peak, with an efficiency of up to 90%. If running the motors at full power (9.5 kW)​
​with a single 3-pack battery system at 1332 Wh, we can expect a total runtime of roughly 8.5​
​minutes. Extensive testing will be done prior to the competition date to verify our speed target​
​and ensure the battery capacity can handle the power requirements of these motors.​
​Each motor is controlled by an ESC, rated for 200 A continuous and 1,000 A peak. The​
​IP67 waterproof rating allows direct marine deployment without additional external sealing.​

pages.text:
​Motor rotation is transmitted via a flex cable drive assembly passing through brass​
​stuffing tubes in the transom with all penetrations epoxied against water ingress. One assembly​
​runs standard left rotation and the other right rotation, counter-rotating the propellers to cancel​
​net torque reaction and improve straight-line tracking.​
​Each shaft is fitted with a CNC-machined 3-blade propeller with a 66 mm diameter and​
​3.64" pitch, hard oxygen-anodized for hardness and corrosion resistance. One propeller is​
​standard rotation and one reversed to match the respective shaft directions [6].​
​Steering is accomplished via a single servo-actuated rudder, angled through a linkage arm​
​at the transom, supplemented by two trim tabs and two turn fins. The trim tabs control pitch trim​
​to maintain an optimal planing angle, and the turn fins provide lateral stability during cornering.​

​Autonomous Controls System​
​The autonomous control system is built around the CubePilot​​®​ ​Cube Orange+ flight​
​controller, which serves as the central processing unit for navigation, motor control, and steering.​
​The Cube Orange+ runs ArduPilot​​®​ ​in Rover mode configured for a motorboat, which supports​
​matched-throttle twin motor output combined with a dedicated servo steering output.​
​Navigation data is handled by a Here3+ GPS module, which provides positional data to​
​the flight controller over CAN bus. Heading is derived from the Cube Orange+'s internal IMUs.​

​ground control software, which communicates with the Cube Orange+ via a pair of RFD 900x​
​radio modems. The RFD 900x link provides the connection between the ground station laptop​
​and the craft, allowing the operator to monitor vehicle state, upload or modify waypoint​

​Build and Fabrication​
​Hull Fabrication​
​The hull was manufactured using a foam plug and fiberglass layup process (Figure 5) to​
​produce a lightweight composite shell with sufficient structural integrity for planing operation. A​
​CNC-machined foam plug was used to define the external geometry, after which multiple layers​
​of fiberglass cloth were applied and bonded using marine-grade epoxy. The layup was​
​vacuum-bagged and cured to ensure consistent fiber wet-out and minimize void formation.​

​Figure 5​. Fiberglass layup manufacturing process​
​Following curing, the hull surface was refined through fairing and sanding to improve​
​geometric fidelity and reduce surface roughness in wetted regions. An additional epoxy layer​
​was applied to seal the surface, improve durability, and enhance hydrodynamic performance.​
​These finishing steps (Figure 6) were necessary to correct minor manufacturing defects and​
​achieve a smooth, continuous outer surface suitable for high-speed operation.​

​Figure 6.​​Hull after fabrication, fairing, sanding, and epoxy application​
​The internal reinforcement structure was assembled separately using laser-cut 1/4”​
​basswood stiffeners. Longitudinal and transverse members were bonded together using epoxy to​
​form a rigid framework, which was then mechanically attached to 3D-printed PETG brackets.​
​Bolted connections between stiffeners and brackets were used to improve load distribution and​
​ensure structural reliability under combined loading.​
​The bracket network was bonded to the hull using epoxy fillets, providing a strong and​
​continuous interface between the composite shell and internal structure. These fillets increase​
​bonding area and reduce stress concentrations, enabling effective transfer of hydrodynamic and​
​structural loads into the reinforcement network. Together, this fabrication and assembly approach​
​produces a lightweight yet robust hull capable of withstanding both distributed and localized​
​loading during operation.​

​Propulsion Fabrication​
​The propulsion system consists of the rudder, flex shafts, pushrod linkage to the tiller,​
​turn fins, trim tabs, stuffing tubes, adjustable strut supports, and counter-rotating left- and​
​right-hand propellers (Figure 7). The flex shafts transmit power from the motors to the propellers​
​and pass through the stuffing tubes. These stuffing tubes are installed by drilling openings​
​through the stern and epoxying the tubes securely in place.​
​The adjustable strut supports are used to set the propeller angle. Each flex shaft passes​
​through its corresponding strut support and connects to the propeller, which is secured using a​
​dog drive fixed to the rotating shaft axis. The trim tabs and turn fins improve the stability and​
​handling of the boat, and they are mounted at the outer edges of the stern using screws, as shown​
​below.​
​The rudder assembly is also screwed on to the boat’s stern. A push rod passes through the​
​boat’s structure to connect the servo with the tiller of the rudder assembly. A gasket is used with​
​the pushrod to prevent any water from seeping into the boat.​

​of the hull volume and internal buoyancy aids in the form of PVC airbags. The hull assembly​
​provides an estimated internal volume of 0.0226 m​​3​​, which corresponds to a buoyant force of​
​approximately 50 lb in freshwater. In addition, five Holt PVC buoyancy bags rated at 15 lb each​

​Risk Mitigation​
           ​Positive buoyancy is ensured by incorporating sufficient displaced air volume to exceed​
​the total weight of the vessel and onboard components. This is achieved through a combination​
​of the hull volume and internal buoyancy aids in the form of PVC airbags. The hull assembly​
​provides an estimated internal volume of 0.0226 m​​3​​, which corresponds to a buoyant force of​
​approximately 50 lb in freshwater. In addition, five Holt PVC buoyancy bags rated at 15 lb each​

pages.text:
​are secured within the hull, providing an additional 75 lb of buoyant capacity. Therefore, in a​
​worst case flooded condition, the total available buoyancy is approximately 125 lb. With an​
​estimated system weight of 100 lb, this yields a buoyancy factor of safety of 1.25. The buoyancy​
​bags are distributed internally to maintain stability and ensure the vessel remains afloat in the​
​event of water ingress.​
​Several electrical safety measures have also been implemented. Properly rated fusing has​
​been installed, and the ESC and wiring have been waterproofed. Sensors are placed in areas less​
​likely to accumulate water and are housed in sealed containers for additional protection.​
​Electrical components are cooled using a water cooling system that draws water through the​
​rudder to cool the ESC. The batteries were tested by the previous team and were not found to​
​overheat. The likely point of failure in the electronics system would be an improperly rated ESC,​
​which has been addressed by selecting components with adequate ratings.​
​The hull structure has been carefully developed for strength and durability. Fairing has​
​been applied to increase toughness, and epoxy has been used to provide effective waterproofing.​
​The vessel will be tested again in a body of water under the expected loading conditions. Models​
​were created in ANSYS​​®​ ​Fluent and Static Structural for CFD and FEA, and the hull was found​
​to have a large factor of safety. To account for wave impacts and slamming loads on the water​
​surface, internal reinforcement was designed in Solidworks​​®​​. Additional structural elements such​
​as bulkheads were incorporated to further strengthen the hull.​
​Water leakage into the structure could occur if holes or damage are present, though this​
​risk has been reduced through multiple layers of fairing and epoxy. Long term operation could​
​lead to cavitation, but this is not a major concern due to the short duration of the competition​
​runs. Loss of GPS signal or degraded data quality could cause the vessel to deviate from its​
​intended path or stop. A failsafe system has been implemented to address this scenario in​
​accordance with the competition rules.​

​planing hull, a reinforced internal structure, twin electric propulsion systems, and an autonomous​
​navigation system based on GPS and IMU data. Engineering analysis, computer simulations, and​

​Conclusion​
        ​This project presents the design and construction of an autonomous electric boat capable​
​of competing in the ASNE Unmanned Autonomy competition. The boat combines a high speed​
​planing hull, a reinforced internal structure, twin electric propulsion systems, and an autonomous​
​navigation system based on GPS and IMU data. Engineering analysis, computer simulations, and​

pages.text:
​hands-on fabrication were used together to create a boat that is lightweight, strong, and suitable​
​for real operating conditions.​
​Safety and reliability were key priorities throughout the design process. Measures such as​
​redundant power systems, proper electrical protection, waterproofing, and built in buoyancy help​
​ensure the boat can remain operational even if problems occur. The control system allows the​
​boat to follow waypoints accurately and includes failsafe behavior if GPS data becomes​
​unreliable or communication is lost.​
​Overall, the final vessel meets the performance goals and technical requirements of the​
​competition while demonstrating reliable autonomous operation on the water. The completed​
​system reflects the team’s work in design, analysis, manufacturing, and testing, and shows that a​
​compact electric platform can successfully perform high speed autonomous navigation in a​
​marine environment.​
